bugs: failed() clears sync_started_at for every id with no check on who owns the claim (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:97-100). If a delayed release is only picked up after retryUntil, by which time the dispatcher may have re-claimed the rows, failed() wipes that newer claim and the rows can be dispatched twice. This is a narrow window.

Marking synced_at with the claim time works at one-second resolution. An edit made after the job reads the rows, but in the same second as the claim, would be counted as synced. In practice this is very unlikely.
antipatterns: app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:84-91 uses (clone $sent) twice to share a builder. This works, but two named queries would read more clearly.
tests/Feature/PushStockAllocationsTest.php:103-106 mocks the queue Job contract with Mockery. withFakeQueueInteractions()/assertReleased() is the idiomatic way to do this.
app/Console/Commands/DispatchStockSync.php:23-28 chains lazyById(100)->pluck->chunk(100). The paging is done twice where one chunkById would do.
strengths: Uses a proactive shared RateLimited middleware backed by the Redis cache, registered in AppServiceProvider, and also reacts to 429 with a capped Retry-After.
Claims rows inside a transaction with lockForUpdate and a re-check of the readyToSync scope, which is safe across servers. The schedule uses onOneServer()->withoutOverlapping(5).

synced_at = sync_started_at (the claim time). A probe confirmed that an edit made while the request is in flight stays ready. A comment records the MySQL left-to-right assignment order, a real constraint that would break if the columns were reordered.
The job filters on whereNotNull('sync_started_at'), so a duplicate SQS delivery does not resend. A probe confirmed only 1 request was sent.
retryUntil is fixed in the constructor and ends before the 15-minute claim expires; MaxExceptions and Backoff are set as attributes. Bookkeeping writes use toBase() so updated_at is not bumped.
Thorough Pest tests: a dataset for the scope, a Retry-After dataset, a schedule assertion, failed() releasing the claim, idempotency, and an index on the migration.

bugs: synced_at is set to $sentAt, which is now() taken after the rows are read (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:50,69). An edit made during the slow HTTP call in the same second gives updated_at == synced_at, so the row is never resent. A probe with frozen time confirmed the change was lost (ready after: false).

handle() does not check that the rows are still claimed (whereNotNull('sync_started_at')). A duplicate SQS delivery or a re-run after success resends the batch to the storefront. A probe confirmed 2 requests were sent.

There is no proactive rate limiting, only a reaction to 429. At a peak of about 50 jobs across three workers' containers the API will keep returning 429, and retries are bounded by the 14-minute retryUntil, so batches may fail and wait for the next dispatch cycle.

The claim is identified by the second-precision value sync_started_at = $claimedAt (app/Console/Commands/DispatchStockSync.php:28-32). Two dispatcher runs in the same second would each pick up the other's rows. Only onOneServer prevents this.
antipatterns: app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:68-72 runs the synced and disabled updates without a transaction.
The migration has no index for the readyToSync filter at scale.
app/Models/StockAllocation.php:30-33 puts a docblock on the scope that documents a convention enforced elsewhere.
strengths: The claim is a conditional UPDATE followed by a re-select, which is compact and avoids explicit locks.
Uses partition() to split missing and accepted rows, which reads cleanly.
The tests use withFakeQueueInteractions()->assertReleased(delay:), travel() for claim expiry, and an in-flight edit test with a different-second edit.
Uses modern attributes (#[Signature], #[Scope], #[Fillable], #[Backoff], #[MaxExceptions], #[Timeout]), and retryUntil is bounded under the claim TTL.
failed() releases the claim, and an end-to-end test re-dispatches the rows afterwards.

v.rationale:
I ran `php artisan test` on both: impl-1 passed 37/37 and impl-2 passed 26/26. I then ran throwaway probe tests on each and deleted them afterwards.

Both share the same overall design: an attribute-based command and job, a readyToSync scope, toBase() writes that leave updated_at alone, onOneServer with withoutOverlapping, retryUntil under the claim TTL, and failed() releasing the claim.

impl-1 is stronger on the task's focus:
- It rate-limits up front with RateLimited middleware backed by the shared limiter, as well as handling 429.
- It claims rows under a transaction with lockForUpdate.
- It uses the claim time as synced_at, so edits made mid-flight are not lost.
- It skips rows that are no longer claimed, so duplicate SQS deliveries do not resend.

impl-2's probes found two real problems. An edit made while the request is in flight, in the same second the job read the row, is permanently lost. A duplicate delivery resends the batch. It also has no proactive rate limiting for a peak of about 5,000 rows, so it relies on 429 retries.

impl-2's tests are slightly more idiomatic in places (withFakeQueueInteractions, travel), but impl-1's tests cover more. impl-1's remaining issues are minor: the Mockery usage, the clone-builder pattern, and a narrow race where failed() can clear a newer claim.
